stem: A 68-year-old woman has knee osteoarthritis with pain on stairs. Exam shows crepitus and mild effusion; she is overweight. What is the MOST appropriate first-line management?
options: Exercise, weight loss and paracetamol/topical NSAID
explanation: Core OA management: exercise (incl. quadriceps strengthening), weight loss, topical NSAIDs and paracetamol; oral NSAIDs add GI/CV risk; surgery after failure of conservative care.
pearl: Move it, lose it, rub it in - before you swallow anything.
trap: Long-term oral NSAIDs in an older overweight patient.

stem: A 58-year-old man with recurrent gout has just had an acute flare in his first MTP joint while taking allopurinol 100 mg daily (started 6 weeks ago). What is the MOST appropriate action?
options: Treat the flare (NSAID/colchicine/steroid) and continue allopurinol at the same dose
Stop allopurinol during the flare and restart after
Increase allopurinol to 300 mg during the flare
Cease allopurinol permanently - it is causing flares
Add a uricosuric agent during the flare
explanation: Flares during initiation are expected: treat the acute attack, continue allopurinol (do not stop), titrate later to urate target, and use prophylaxis for 6 months.
pearl: Do not stop ULT for a flare - ride it out with flare therapy.
trap: Stopping the ULT resets the titration clock and guarantees more flares.

stem: A 45-year-old woman has 8 weeks of symmetrical small-joint pain and stiffness lasting 90 minutes. What is the MOST appropriate management?
options: Prompt referral for early rheumatology assessment (DMARDs within weeks)
Trial of NSAIDs and review in 6 months
Serology first, and refer only if both RF and anti-CCP are positive
explanation: Suspected early RA: urgent rheumatology referral for DMARD initiation (window of opportunity); X-ray changes are late; seronegative RA exists.
pearl: Refer clinically - early DMARDs prevent deformity.
trap: Waiting for erosions on X-ray.

stem: A 72-year-old woman has 4 weeks of shoulder and pelvic girdle stiffness, worse in the morning, with an ESR of 62. What is the MOST appropriate initial therapy?
options: Prednisolone ~15 mg daily with rapid symptom response expected within days
explanation: PMR responds dramatically to low-dose prednisolone (10-20 mg) within days; 60 mg suggests GCA dosing; NSAIDs are ineffective.
pearl: A rapid dramatic response is itself diagnostic support.
trap: Giant-cell arteritis dosing for pure PMR.

stem: A 74-year-old woman with PMR develops a new temporal headache, jaw claudication and blurred vision. What is the MOST appropriate immediate action?
options: Start high-dose oral corticosteroids immediately and arrange same-day ophthalmology
Arrange temporal artery biopsy before any treatment
CT head first, steroids only if positive
explanation: Suspected GCA with visual symptoms: immediate high-dose steroids BEFORE any investigation - biopsy can follow (weeks later and still valid); delay risks permanent blindness.
pearl: Steroids now, biopsy later.
trap: Waiting for biopsy confirmation while the sight is lost.

stem: A 55-year-old man has 3 months of shoulder pain, painful arc, and weakness of abduction against resistance. What is the MOST appropriate initial management?
options: Analgesia and a structured rotator-cuff exercise program (physiotherapy)
Cortisone injection as first step for everyone
explanation: Most rotator cuff pathology responds to a structured exercise program; imaging/injections are selected later, surgery after failed conservative care.
pearl: Rehab before referral; injection is not the default.
trap: MRI-first thinking for a mechanical problem that needs exercise.

stem: A 22-year-old man inverts his ankle playing football. He can bear weight immediately and there is tenderness only over the lateral malleolus with no bone tenderness at the posterior edge or tips. What is the MOST appropriate management?
options: RICE and early mobilisation; no X-ray required by Ottawa rules
Immobilisation in a cast for 6 weeks
explanation: Ottawa ankle rules: X-ray only if bone tenderness at malleolar tips/posterior edge, or inability to bear weight 4 steps. Otherwise functional management.
pearl: The rules exist so you do not radiograph every sprain.
trap: Reflex X-rays for every twisted ankle.

stem: A 68-year-old woman on alendronate for 5 years asks how long she must continue. DEXA today: T-score -2.6, no fractures since treatment. What is the MOST appropriate advice?
options: Review at 5 years: consider a drug holiday only if fracture risk is now low, otherwise continue
Stop immediately - 5 years always cures it
Continue for life without review in every case
explanation: At 5 years on a bisphosphonate, reassess fracture risk: low-risk patients may take a drug holiday with monitoring; higher-risk patients continue (or switch agents).
pearl: Five years: re-check risk before renewing the prescription.
trap: Automatic lifelong therapy without reassessment.

stem: A family of four has intense night-time itch with burrows in the finger webs; the 6-month-old baby has palm involvement. What is the MOST appropriate management?
options: Permethrin 5% for all members and close contacts simultaneously, with laundering of bedding and clothing
explanation: Scabies: treat all household/close contacts simultaneously (even asymptomatic - incubation means they carry it), plus hot-wash linens; permethrin is first-line including infants at appropriate dosing intervals.
pearl: Treat the household the same day, not just the itchy ones.
trap: Treating only the index case - instant reinfestation.

stem: A 40-year-old man presents with a 7 mm irregular pigmented lesion on his back with varied colours and recent change in size over 3 months. What is the MOST appropriate management?
options: Excision biopsy with a 2 mm margin and dermoscopic/histological assessment
explanation: Any lesion suspicious for melanoma needs complete excisional biopsy (2 mm clinical margin) - partial sampling (shave) compromises staging; cryotherapy and imiquimod are never for possible melanoma.
pearl: Cut it out whole - never shave a possible melanoma.
trap: Watching a changing pigmented lesion for 6 months.

stem: A 6-month-old infant has widespread flexural eczema affecting sleep. Parents use emollient twice weekly and fear steroid creams. What is the MOST appropriate advice?
options: Daily thick emollients plus an appropriate-strength topical corticosteroid for flares, with explanation that steroids used correctly are safe
Avoid all steroids - they thin skin permanently
explanation: Eczema: liberal daily emollients + adequately strong topical steroids for flares (undertreatment is the main problem); address steroid phobia directly with education.
pearl: Under-treating with steroid phobia causes more harm than steroids ever will.
trap: Homeopathic-strength steroid use for a severe flare.

stem: A 35-year-old man has chronic plaques on elbows and scalp; nail pitting is present. Topical steroids give partial relief. What is the MOST appropriate next step?
options: Add a vitamin-D analogue (calcipotriol) in combination with the steroid, and review
explanation: First-line for chronic plaque psoriasis: combination topical steroid + calcipotriol; systemic therapy is for severe/refractory disease; solarium is never therapy.
pearl: Steroid + vitamin D analogue beats either alone.
trap: Systemic steroids causing rebound pustular psoriasis.

stem: An 18-year-old woman has moderate papulopustular acne with some nodules, unresponsive to 3 months of topical benzoyl peroxide. She is on a levonorgestrel pill. What is the MOST appropriate next step?
options: Add a topical retinoid and consider switching to an anti-androgenic pill; isotretinoin if severe/refractory
No treatment - she will grow out of it
explanation: Moderate acne failing topical monotherapy: combination topical (retinoid + BPO ± antibiotic) and hormonal options (switching OCP); isotretinoin reserved for severe or refractory disease.
pearl: Step up combinations before escalating to isotretinoin.
trap: Antibiotics for acne as a solo long-term strategy.

stem: A 25-year-old contact-lens wearer has 2 days of a painful red right eye with photophobia and tearing; vision is slightly reduced. He sleeps in his lenses. What is the MOST appropriate action?
options: Topical antibiotic from the chemist and review tomorrow
Eye patch and review next week
Stop the lenses and observe for a week
explanation: Pain + photophobia + reduced vision + contact lens wear = microbial keratitis until proven otherwise: same-day ophthalmology (scraping/cultures, intensive drops). Delay can mean perforation.
pearl: Contact lens + painful red eye = cornea, same day.
trap: Chemist chloramphenicol for a sight-threatening keratitis.

stem: A 66-year-old woman has 6 hours of severe right eye pain, haloes around lights, vomiting, a hazy cornea and a mid-dilated fixed pupil. What is the MOST appropriate action?
options: Miotic drops then wait a week
explanation: Acute angle closure is an ophthalmic emergency (permanent visual loss within days): emergency referral for medical therapy (drops, acetazolamide) and laser iridotomy.
pearl: Painful red eye + haloes + vomiting = angle closure, today.
trap: Mistaking it for migraine or gastroenteritis.

stem: A 55-year-old myopic man describes a sudden shower of floaters then a 'curtain' over the left visual field. What is the MOST appropriate action?
options: Oral NSAIDs and bed rest at home
explanation: New floater shower + curtain field loss = retinal detachment: same-day assessment. Days matter for macular involvement.
pearl: A curtain over the vision is an emergency, not a floater.
trap: Watchful waiting for acute PVD features.

unit: Ear, nose, throat and oral health
stem: A 2-year-old has 48 hours of bilateral ear pain, fever 38.5, and both drums are red and bulging. She is distressed but systemically well. What is the MOST appropriate management?
options: Analgesia plus a wait-and-watch approach with a safety-net prescription or review in 48 hours
explanation: Most AOM in children over 6 months is viral or self-limiting: analgesia-first with deferred antibiotics (delayed script/review), reserving immediate antibiotics for systemically unwell children, under-6-months, or specific contexts.
pearl: Analgesia first; antibiotics on a short leash.
trap: Antibiotics reflexively for every red drum.

unit: Ear, nose, throat and oral health
stem: A 32-year-old swimmer has 3 days of an itchy, painful ear canal with debris and pain on touching the tragus; the drum is normal. What is the MOST appropriate management?
options: Topical antibiotic-steroid drops (aural toilet if the canal permits)
explanation: Otitis externa: topical combination drops (antibiotic + steroid) ± aural toilet; keep the ear dry; oral antibiotics only for cellulitis/immunosuppression.
pearl: Topical therapy for a topical disease.
trap: Oral antibiotics as first-line (and resistance).

unit: Ear, nose, throat and oral health
stem: A 58-year-old man on aspirin has an anterior nosebleed for 15 minutes. He is haemodynamically stable. What is the FIRST step?
options: Sit him upright, lean forward, and apply continuous firm pressure to the soft nasal cartilage for 10-20 minutes
Lie him down with head back
explanation: First aid first: upright, lean forward, pinch the soft part (Little's area) without interruption for 10-20 minutes; then assess (and cautery if a visible vessel once bleeding controlled).
pearl: Pressure before packing; leaning forward not back.
trap: Tipping the head back - blood swallowed, airway risk.

stem: A 19-year-old has 12 hours of fever, severe headache, neck stiffness and a new petechial rash. What is the MOST appropriate action?
options: Oral antibiotics at home then review in 4 hours
explanation: Fever + meningism + petechiae = meningococcal disease: emergency transfer. In the community, give IV/IM antibiotics (per state guidance, e.g., ceftriaxone) before transfer if it will not delay it.
pearl: Petechiae plus meningism: ambulance, antibiotics, now.
trap: Waiting in a waiting room queue.

stem: A 3-year-old has 6 days of fever despite amoxicillin, red eyes without discharge, cracked red lips, swollen hands, and a unilateral neck node. What is the MOST appropriate action?
options: Urgent referral for IV immunoglobulin within 10 days of illness onset
Continue antibiotics for a further week
explanation: Fever ≥5 days plus mucositis, conjunctival injection, extremity changes and lymphadenopathy = Kawasaki disease: urgent referral for IVIG (before day 10 to prevent coronary aneurysms).
pearl: Fever five days plus red everything: think Kawasaki, refer today.
trap: A second antibiotic course for a non-bacterial illness.

stem: A 7-month-old has coryza, then 3 days of cough, mild recession and poor feeding. SpO2 94% in air, no apnoea, feeding about 60% of normal. What is the MOST appropriate management?
options: Supportive care at home with clear safety-netting
explanation: Bronchiolitis: supportive care; bronchodilators, steroids, antibiotics and CXR are NOT routine. Home care is appropriate if feeding ≥50%, SpO2 adequate and parents confident.
pearl: Feed them, watch them, bring them back if worse - but no drugs.
trap: Salbutamol for a viral infant wheeze.

stem: A 4-year-old girl has dysuria and frequency; a clean-catch urine shows leucocytes and nitrites. She is afebrile and well. What is the MOST appropriate management?
options: Treat as a lower UTI (e.g., trimethoprim per local resistance) and arrange a follow-up sample; no routine imaging for a single uncomplicated infection
explanation: Afebrile well child with lower UTI: short-course antibiotics and a follow-up test of cure; imaging is for atypical/recurrent infections or infants.
pearl: Treat, confirm clearance, image only when the story is not simple.
trap: Automatic ultrasound for every first UTI.

stem: A 7-year-old still wets the bed most nights, by day he is dry and otherwise well. What is the MOST appropriate first-line management?
explanation: First-line for uncomplicated nocturnal enuresis (≥7 years): alarm therapy with parental engagement; desmopressin when alarms fail or rapid/short-term control is needed.
pearl: Alarms first; drugs are the backup.
trap: Fluid restriction to the point of dehydration.

stem: An 8-year-old boy has pervasive inattention and impulsivity at home AND school for over a year, impairing learning and friendships. What is the MOST appropriate pathway?
options: Referral for comprehensive assessment (paediatrics/psychology) using multiple informants
explanation: ADHD requires comprehensive multi-informant assessment (home + school tools, exclusion of mimics) through specialist services before treatment; GPs coordinate and support but assessment comes first.
pearl: Two settings, two informants, one thorough assessment.
trap: Stimulants on a single teacher's note.

stem: An 81-year-old man has 6 months of low mood, poor sleep, and reduced function after his wife died. He scored 21/30 on a cognitive screen last week. What is the MOST important next step?
options: Distinguish depression from dementia (including pseudodementia) with collateral history and treat depression (psychotherapy/SSRI as appropriate)
explanation: Depression in older people often mimics dementia (pseudodementia): collateral history, depression-focused treatment and monitoring cognition over time - it frequently improves with mood treatment.
pearl: Depressed cognition can look demented - treat the mood and re-test.
trap: Locking in a dementia label during bereavement depression.

stem: An 85-year-old woman has had 3 falls in 6 months. She takes ramipril, amlodipine, temazepam and doxazosin; lying BP 142/80, standing 110/68 with dizziness. What is the MOST appropriate intervention?
options: Deprescribe the temazepam and doxazosin, review antihypertensives, add strength-balance exercise and vision check
Fear of falling is protective - discourage activity
explanation: Falls: review culprit sedatives/vasodilators FIRST, then exercise (balance/strength), vision, footwear, home hazards; vitamin D if deficient. Avoid over-treating BP in the frail.
pearl: Stop the drugs that drop her before she drops.
trap: Bed rest and further deconditioning.

stem: A family calls about their 84-year-old father in a residential facility: overnight he became acutely confused and agitated. Last week he had a UTI treated. What is the MOST appropriate initial approach?
options: Assess for acute causes (infection, drugs, retention, hypoxia, metabolic), manage environment, treat the cause
Start an antipsychotic immediately and move on
Diagnose dementia and update the family
explanation: Delirium = acute fluctuating confusion: look hard for the driver (infection, drugs esp. anticholinergics, retention, hypoxia, electrolytes) and use non-pharmacologic management first; antipsychotics only if danger/distress.
pearl: Confusion that changed overnight is delirium until proven otherwise.
trap: Sedation before searching for the cause.

stem: An 80-year-old man has repeat 'falls' with explanations that change each time. His son insists on being present at every appointment and answers for him. Weight is down 4 kg. What is the MOST appropriate next step?
options: See him alone, ask directly and sensitively about safety and mistreatment, and know your reporting options
Confront the son in the room
Order more CT scans for the falls
explanation: Red flags for elder abuse: changing explanations, caregiver controlling the consultation, weight loss, delay in care. See the patient alone, ask directly, document, and use state pathways (QLD: adult safeguarding/unit via Elder Abuse Helpline).
pearl: Get the controller out of the room and ask.
trap: Confrontation in the room, endangering the patient.

stem: An 86-year-old woman takes 14 medications including two antihypertensives, an anticholinergic bladder drug, and nighttime temazepam. She is dizzy in the mornings and has had one fall. What is the MOST appropriate approach?
options: Structured deprescribing review prioritising fall-risk drugs (sedatives, vasodilators, anticholinergics)
Continue all - stopping medications is risky
Add a drug for the dizziness
explanation: Multimorbidity guidelines: prioritise harms over marginal benefits in the frail old; stepwise deprescribing of fall-risk drugs with monitoring.
pearl: Every new symptom in the elderly is a drug side-effect until proven otherwise.
trap: Prescribing for drug-induced illness with another drug.

stem: A 78-year-old man with severe COPD attends with his daughter. He asks about future care planning while well. What is the MOST appropriate approach?
options: Facilitate advance care planning discussion: goals, surrogate decision-maker, documented plan and limits of treatment
Tell him it is too early to discuss
explanation: ACP early in chronic serious illness: explore values, appoint a substitute decision-maker (QLD: enduring power of attorney / statutory health attorney), document, share with the team.
pearl: Plan while stable, not in the crisis.
trap: Reducing ACP to a CPR tick-box.

stem: A terminally ill patient on 60 mg oral morphine daily has 2-3 breakthrough pain episodes daily. What is the appropriate breakthrough dose?
options: Approximately 10-15 mg oral morphine (about 1/6 of the total daily dose)
60 mg - the same as the daily dose
No analgesia - avoid addiction near death
explanation: Breakthrough opioid = about 1/6 of the TOTAL daily dose, adjusted by response. Undertreatment of terminal pain is the greater harm; addiction is not a palliative end-stage concern.
pearl: One-sixth of the daily dose, every breakthrough.
trap: Same-as-daily dosing causing overdose.

stem: In Queensland, which of the following is required for voluntary assisted dying eligibility?
options: Adult Queensland resident with decision-making capacity, intolerable suffering from an advanced progressive condition, and the statutory request process completed
Any adult with chronic pain wanting to die
Family request on the patient's behalf
explanation: QLD VAD (since 2023): adult, resident, capacity, suffering intolerably from a qualifying advanced/progressive condition expected to cause death, undergoing the formal request/assessment process with coordinating and independent practitioners.
pearl: Capacity is a VAD prerequisite throughout the process.
trap: Family-initiated requests or losing capacity and still proceeding.

stem: A dependent drinker (100 g/day) is admitted for an unrelated surgery; withdrawal risk is high. What is the MOST appropriate management?
options: A benzodiazepine withdrawal regimen (e.g., diazepam per CIWA-Ar) plus thiamine BEFORE any glucose
explanation: Prevent withdrawal: symptom-triggered benzodiazepines (CIWA-Ar), thiamine BEFORE any glucose-containing fluids, monitor electrolytes; naltrexone/disulfiram are relapse-prevention, not withdrawal drugs.
pearl: Thiamine before toast, tea or TPN.
trap: Glucose before thiamine precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy.

stem: A 50-year-old smoker with COPD wants to quit next month. What is the MOST effective pharmacotherapy approach?
options: Varenicline (or combination NRT) plus behavioural support with a quit date
Nicotine patch alone at half dose
explanation: Behavioural support + pharmacotherapy doubles quit rates: varenicline most effective for many (or combination NRT patch + PRN); set a quit date and follow-up within a week.
pearl: Drugs + a date + follow-up - all three or it fizzles.
trap: Vaping as a doctor-endorsed first-line stop-smoking medicine.

stem: A 30-year-old man with heroin dependence wants treatment. Which option is the FIRST-LINE maintenance therapy in Australia?
options: Buprenorphine (or methadone) via an accredited prescriber, with psychosocial support
Methadone from any GP without accreditation
explanation: Opioid agonist therapy (buprenorphine or methadone) with accredited prescribing and wraparound psychosocial care is the evidence-based maintenance approach; detox alone has high relapse and overdose risk.
pearl: Maintenance beats detox for staying alive.
trap: Unsupported detox - fatal overdose risk post-discharge.

stem: A 68-year-old man asks about PSA testing. He is asymptomatic with no family history. What is the MOST appropriate advice?
options: Offer an informed-choice discussion: PSA testing may detect cancer earlier but risks overdiagnosis and overtreatment; if testing, consent to the trade-offs first
Test annually without discussion from 50 years
Start PSA at 40 in all men
PSA is a yes/no cancer test
explanation: PSA: no population screening programme; RACGP advises informed decision-making (benefits vs overdiagnosis/overtreatment harms) for men from 50 (45 with family history). Testing only after consent to the conversation.
pearl: Consent to the test includes consent to its consequences.
trap: Reflexive annual PSA from 45 without any discussion.

stem: A 56-year-old man has 12 months of erectile dysfunction. He smokes and has borderline hypertension. What is the MOST appropriate initial evaluation?
options: Cardiovascular risk assessment (ED is a marker of endothelial disease), plus focused exam, testosterone if libido low, then PDE5 inhibitor if suitable
explanation: ED is often the first sign of CVD: assess risk factors, screen for depression, check testosterone if low libido, then PDE5 inhibitors as first-line therapy with contraindication checks (nitrates).
pearl: The penis is a cardiovascular stress test.
trap: Sildenafil without asking about nitrates or the heart.

stem: A 15-year-old has 3 hours of sudden severe right testicular pain with vomiting; the testis is high-lying and exquisitely tender. What is the MOST appropriate action?
options: Immediate surgical referral (ED) - torsion is a time-critical emergency
explanation: Torsion: sudden pain + vomiting + high-riding testis = theatre within hours; imaging must not delay surgery (perfusion lost within 6-8 hours).
pearl: Suspected torsion: straight to theatre, no detours.
trap: Waiting for an ultrasound while the testis dies.

stem: A 22-year-old asymptomatic man who has sex with men requests a sexual health check. What is the MOST appropriate testing set (per Australian STI guidelines)?
options: NAAT for chlamydia and gonorrhoea at relevant sites (urine/rectal/pharyngeal per exposure), HIV and syphilis serology
explanation: Asymptomatic MSM screen: site-specific NAATs for chlamydia/gonorrhoea (urine, pharyngeal, anal as exposure dictates), HIV serology (4th-gen), and syphilis serology, at least 6-12 monthly depending on risk.
pearl: Test the sites that were exposed - not just the urine.
trap: Urine-only testing missing rectal and pharyngeal infection.

stem: A 30-year-old pregnant woman's syphilis screen (EIA) is reactive. What is the MOST appropriate next step?
options: Confirm with a second different serological test and treponemal-specific testing, and refer for treatment urgently - congenital syphilis risk
Reassure as EIA often false positive
Repeat the same EIA in 6 months
No treatment if she has no symptoms
explanation: Reactive screening syphilis: confirm with different assays (treponemal + non-treponemal e.g., RPR for activity) and treat promptly in pregnancy - congenital syphilis is rising in Australia and penicillin is the treatment.
pearl: Screen positive in pregnancy: confirm, stage, treat, fast.
trap: Reassurance during a rising congenital syphilis era.
